prompt.brief: Design a weather service that aggregates provider observations and forecasts, serves current conditions and multi-day outlooks, and delivers timely location-aware alerts with freshness metadata.
successSignals: Define provider normalization, station/grid identity, forecast versions, units, timezone, freshness, confidence, and alert lifecycle.
Cache by geospatial cell and forecast horizon, refresh adaptively, reconcile conflicting providers, and avoid thundering-herd refreshes.
Separate provider ingestion from serving projections, historical observations, notifications, and expensive forecast transformations.
Explain provider outage, stale labeling, alert deduplication, location privacy, observability, and degraded cached forecasts.

functional: Return current conditions, hourly/daily forecasts, historical observations, air-quality fields, units, and provider/freshness metadata.
Subscribe users to threshold/severe-weather alerts by location, deduplicate notifications, and support locale/timezone preferences.
Ingest multiple providers, retry safely, backfill gaps, invalidate outdated forecasts, and serve cached data with an explicit stale marker.
nonFunctional: Serve common forecast reads with p95 under 200ms and propagate severe alerts within two minutes of provider receipt.
Scale to 50M users and highly skewed popular locations without a single hot key or unbounded synchronous work.
Do not lose committed state; make retries and duplicate events safe.
Degrade safely when downstream workers, caches, or external dependencies fail.
scaleAssumptions: 50M users, 10M watched locations, and 1M provider updates per hour
Partition by the primary tenant, user, item, or geographic key and isolate hot partitions.
Keep serving state bounded; retain raw events or durable records for replay and auditing.

architecture.title: Weather Application domain architecture
architecture.summary: Design a weather service that aggregates provider observations and forecasts, serves current conditions and multi-day outlooks, and delivers timely location-aware alerts with freshness metadata. The design makes weather application decisions durable, isolates slow or external work behind replayable boundaries, and exposes freshness, authorization, and recovery state to operators and clients.

layers.label: Forecast query plane
layers.description: Clients receive location-aware forecasts and explicit freshness or quality state.

layers.label: Provider ingestion and normalization
layers.description: External feeds become canonical, versioned observations and forecasts.

layers.label: Time and spatial forecast truth

layers.label: Alerts and forecast quality

layers.label: Weather reliability operations
layers.description: Feed gaps, freshness, and alert signals protect user trust.

deepDives.title: Provider freshness and gaps
points: Carry provider issue time, valid time, fetch time, cursor, and signature through the model.
Expose spatial coverage and stale state instead of silently filling a missing provider feed.
Use provider adapters so schema or quota failures are isolated.

deepDives.title: Time and spatial indexing
points: Partition by geospatial cell and valid-time bucket for bounded forecast reads.
Keep forecast revisions separate from observations so consumers can compare what was known when.
Cache only with a provider watermark and expiry contract.

deepDives.title: Alert correctness
points: Evaluate thresholds with hysteresis, deduplication, and subscription version to prevent alert storms.
Record the forecast or observation evidence behind each alert.
Track delivery latency, suppressed duplicates, and stale-policy behavior.

tradeoffs.title: Provider redundancy versus cost
tradeoffs.recommendation: Use multiple providers for severe-weather or high-availability paths and a single source for lower-risk products.
tradeoffs.caution: Failover without normalization or confidence metadata can produce contradictory forecasts.

tradeoffs.title: Precompute tiles versus query on demand
tradeoffs.recommendation: Precompute common spatial/time products and compute rare views within a bounded budget.
tradeoffs.caution: Generating every resolution and time horizon is expensive and hard to invalidate.

tradeoffs.title: Freshness versus stability
tradeoffs.recommendation: Expose issued and valid times and choose product-specific freshness budgets.
tradeoffs.caution: Aggressively refreshing can amplify provider rate limits without improving forecast quality.

commonMistakes: Treating fetch success as forecast quality.
Mixing provider issue time with valid time and serving a revision as current without metadata.
Firing duplicate alerts for every forecast revision.
Ignoring spatial gaps, quota failures, and stale caches.
Dropping provider provenance so quality cannot be reconciled later.

followUps.question: How do you handle a provider outage?
followUps.answer: Serve the last acceptable version with explicit freshness, switch to a normalized fallback when policy allows, and alert on coverage gaps.

followUps.question: How do you avoid alert storms?
followUps.answer: Version subscriptions, apply hysteresis and deduplication, and require a new evidence threshold before re-notifying.

followUps.question: How do you measure forecast quality?
followUps.answer: Join forecast versions to later observations by location and valid time, then compute accuracy and coverage by provider and cohort.

The answer partitions weather application traffic, isolates hot keys, and moves fan-out, retries, or rebuilds behind bounded asynchronous work.
